Marquis de Lafayette. Gilbert du Motier was born in 1757, a noble reformer and military hero who championed both the American and French Revolutions. He served without pay as a general in George Washington's army, becoming one of the American Revolution's heroes while he lobbied France to support the cause. When he returned to France in 1785, he played a key role in summoning the Estates-General, hoping to establish a constitutional monarchy and protect citizens' rights. As the French Revolution began, he authored the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen in 1789, one of the revolution's founding documents that reflected his faith in universal rights and law. He also commanded the National Guard during the early revolution, defending the royal family during the Women's March on Versailles in October 1789, trying to preserve both order and reform. But his moderate vision of constitutional monarchy alienated him from both royalists and republicans. The radicals saw him as not revolutionary enough, while royalists viewed him with suspicion. When the radical phase of the revolution began in 1792, he made the fatal political decision to flee France, fearing arrest. He was captured by Austrians and spent the next five years imprisoned. His early idealism and ultimate marginalization made him a symbol of how the revolution transformed from liberal reform into ideological terror. He died in 1834, a relic of an earlier, more hopeful time.
